power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Suicide imagery subtypes and their relationships with suicide behaviour: a mixedmethods evaluation

text.text: Mental imagery about suicide is a commonly experienced risk factor for suicide, but subtypes and their relationships to behaviour remain largely unexplored.
This study aims to identify and describe common themes in suicide imagery content, perceived function, and subjective meaning in relation to suicide behaviour.

Participants (N=20) provided quantitative and qualitative data about content, perceived function, and subjective meaning across 30 unique instances of suicide imagery via online surveys and semi-structured interviews.

Analysis resulted in five key themes: (a) Determination imagery depicting a single action script detailing a chosen suicide method, (b) Solution imagery highlighting wanted impacts of suicide, (c) Mental Exercise or fantasy imagery, (d) Discouraging imagery of unwanted impacts of suicide, and (e) Consideration imagery weighing up different methods.
Determination and Solution imagery were commonly associated with suicide behaviour.
Imagery prior to attempt was often deliberately constructed, wanted, and prolonged (Median duration = 90 minutes).
Findings suggest that imagery themes may vary on dimensions reflecting facilitation and deterrence of behaviour, which may interact to produce ambivalence.
In addition to volitional impacts via suicide action script rehearsal, suicide imagery may increase motivation towards suicide.
Prior to attempt, suicide imagery may be acceptable, comforting, or even sought after.
This study provides a nuanced understanding of suicide imagery subtypes in relation to suicide behaviour and provides a framework to assist clinicians in assessment and formulation.
• Imagery subtypes vary in facilitation and deterrence of suicide behaviour.
• Facilitating imagery can provide action scripts and/or boost motivation to suicide.
• Imagery before attempt may be deliberate, wanted and prolonged; not only intrusive.

Suicide is a major health crisis claiming over 700,000 lives globally each year (Davis Weaver et al., 2025), but the efficacy of existing treatments has shown minimal improvement over the past five decades (Fox, Huang, et al., 2020).

text.text: A greater understanding of modifiable cognitive markers and drivers of suicide risk is needed to inform novel intervention development.
One such cognitive factor is suicide mental imagery (Holmes et al., 2007; Lawrence et al., 2023; O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).

text.text: Current clinical risk assessment and interventions for suicidal ideation focus almost exclusively on verbal thoughts (e.g., "I will [method] on Tuesday night when the house is empty").
text.formatted: Current clinical risk assessment and interventions for suicidal ideation focus almost exclusively on verbal thoughts (e.g., "I will <ref type="bibr">[method]</ref> on Tuesday night when the house is empty").

text.text: Yet, growing evidence indicates that mental imagery of suicide (e.g., mentally imagining suicide behaviours in sensory detail) is a prevalent symptom (74% in clinical samples) (Lawrence et al., 2023) and potential driver of suicide risk, more so than verbal ideation (Wetherall et al., 2018).

text.text: However, no existing studies have evaluated whether suicide imagery varies in relation to the presence or absence of attempt behaviour.
This knowledge is crucial for the development of testable hypotheses regarding suicide imagery mechanisms and the development of targeted interventions.

Mental imagery refers to the internal perception of sensory information in the absence of sensory input (Kosslyn et al., 2001), including visual experiences, sound, and even kinaesthesia (Andrade et al., 2014).

text.text: Imagery-based thoughts evoke stronger emotional and motivational responses (Holmes & Mathews, 2005; Ji et al., 2021; Wicken et al., 2021), increase performance of imagined motor behaviours (Rannaud Monany et al., 2022), and increase the likelihood of completing avoided behaviours with motivational barriers (Ji et al., 2021; Renner et al., 2019) compared to verbal thoughts.

text.text: Imagery-based interventions are supported across contexts including psychological disorders (Blackwell, 2021; Kroener et al., 2023), physical rehabilitation (Rannaud Monany et al., 2022), behaviour change (May et al., 2015), and athlete performance enhancement (Cumming & Hall, 2002).

text.text: In suicide, imagery-based ideation has been associated with an increased likelihood of both having a plan and previously attempting suicide compared to verbal thoughts, and prospectively predicts severity of ideation (Lawrence et al., 2023; Lawrence et al., 2022; Ng et al., 2016; Wetherall et al., 2018).

text.text: Disrupting suicide imagery via visuospatial competing tasks such as eye-movements has shown promise as an adjunct alongside treatment as usual for reducing suicide intention (van Bentum et al., 2017).

text.text: However, efforts to develop evidence-based interventions are hampered by the heterogeneity of suicide imagery and lack of an evidence-based framework for understanding the functional impact.

Mental imagery about suicide can include varied content (Holmes et al., 2007), be associated with a range of subjective appraisals (Holmes et al., 2007), and lead to a range of emotional responses (Crane et al., 2012). Hales et al. (2011) described examples of suicide method imagery that were associated with inclination towards behaviour for some individuals, but discouraged others.

text.text: There has been no in-depth study comparing suicide imagery when intention was acted upon versus when it was not acted upon.
One limiting methodological factor is the assessment of suicide imagery.
The most frequently used tool is the Suicide Cognitions Interview (SCI; Holmes et al., 2007), which has enabled in-depth mapping of the range of suicide imagery experiences.

text.text: However, all items are anchored to a time when the participant was "most despairing or suicidal" (Holmes et al., 2007, p. 426), limiting comparison of imagery characteristics in relation to the enaction of, or refrainment from, suicide behaviours.

text.text: A retrospective study of self-harm (McEvoy et al., 2017) compared cognitions on instances of self-harm to instances where the participant did not self-harm.

text.text: Prior to engaging in nonsuicidal self-injury, imagery tended to be more comforting, to depict self-harm behaviours, and to be appraised as encouraging of self-harm.
In contrast, imagery during episodes when an urge was not acted upon was more distressing and tended to depict negative impacts of self-harm.
This approach represents a feasible method for mapping differences in imagery as a function of behaviour.
To date, no equivalent evaluations have been conducted with suicide imagery.
This study compares the content and characteristics of suicide imagery preceding attempt to imagery not associated with immediate attempt behaviour.
The primary aim is to identify common themes in the content, perceived function, and subjective meaning of suicide imagery in relation to suicide behaviours.
Secondarily, the study aims to describe the broader characteristics of suicide imagery in relation to suicide behaviour.
This study is part of the Qualitative SUicide IMagery (QSUIM) project.
Findings relating to precipitating stressors and behavioural responses to suicide imagery will be reported elsewhere.

This project was conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the University of New South Wales Human Research Ethics Committee (approval number HC230455) and all participants provided informed consent.
Qualitative and quantitative data from a semi-structured interview was supplemented by quantitative demographic and suicidality data to characterise participants.

Two Lived Experience Advisors were paid for their time in sharing decision-making regarding study design, materials, and safety protocols via a written material review and a two-hour workshop with the lead researcher.
Although both advisors were offered the opportunity to contribute to data analysis and manuscript preparation, neither was engaging in advisory work at the time.

English-speaking adults (>18 years) residing in Australia who experienced suicide imagery were recruited via online advertisements in newsletters and social media posts followed by male-focused advertisements to increase male recruitment.

text.text: Two subgroups included: (a) individuals describing imagery without suicide behaviour (non-attempt imagery), and (b) individuals describing both (i) non-attempt imagery and (ii) imagery followed by suicide behaviour (attempt imagery).
Individuals were excluded if they had experienced active suicide intent, preparation, or behaviour within the past 4 weeks, and were provided with information about support services and helplines.
The study utilised purposive sampling to ensure diversity across gender and attempt behaviours (attempt versus non-attempt imagery).
To determine sufficient sample size, the notion of saturation of novel ideas (Saunders et al., 2018) was applied.

text.text: Intrusiveness.
Across the sample, suicide imagery was mostly reported to onset spontaneously.
Half of the attempt imagery instances included some degree of deliberate construction, while non-attempt imagery included deliberate construction less than a quarter of the time.
Once in mind, attempt imagery was experienced as welcome and wanted in most instances, while non-attempt imagery was wanted about half of the time (Table 6).

Attempt imagery was retrospectively perceived to increase suicide urges in most instances, while non-attempt imagery was almost never reported to increase suicide urges (Table 6).

text.text: Six participants spontaneously reported changes in their suicide imagery across time.
Four participants reported that their suicide imagery onset between the ages of 10 and 20 years old, with three reporting persistence in this imagery across decades of their life.
Three reported increases in their suicide imagery over time.
Five themes of suicide imagery were identified and charted onto cases of suicide behaviour (Table 7).

text.text: Participants could experience a combination of imagery themes within a single episode.
Suicide imagery reflecting determination or resolution to suicide ('determination/resolution imagery') frequently co-occurred with attempt behaviour.
This imagery primarily depicted a single method of suicide behaviour or a single suicide plan, which we termed a suicide action script.

These suicide action scripts tended to be extremely detailed ("down to what I was wearing", "exactly how...and where"), highly realistic, and portrayed methods that were feasible, accessible, and lethal.

They often included preparatory behaviours (e.g. preparing materials or how to leave home without alerting family) and were reported to feel mechanical and unemotional ("very matter of fact"), in contrast to the emotional methods in Mental Exercise Imagery.

Two participants described suicide action scripts becoming more detailed and salient immediately preceding attempt ("right before I did it was the strongest"; "The longer I went into it, there was more detail").
In contrast, suicide action scripts not associated with attempt behaviour tended to be less detailed (e.g., fewer details regarding clothing, items, scene details) and omitted preparatory behaviours.

The reported meaning of determination/resolution imagery tended to be passive and conveyed resignation to suicide as inevitable, or as a single path with lack of choice ("I had no choice…This is just what is being done" and "I just wanted to die").

Two participants described the perceived function as pre-experiencing -a passive and automatic mental experiencing of their imminent suicide attempt which subjectively felt like a video "replay" as seen in sports games.
This contrasts with the active planning in Solution Imagery.
Some suicide action scripts were cued by incidental exposure to method-related stimuli (e.g., encountering method implements/locations while running errands).
Such stimulus-cued intrusions were often accompanied by imperative verbal phrases about lethality and accessibility that encouraged action ("I could just"; "I can just do it"; "I could do it").

Two participants noted being surprised on reflection that determination imagery did not contain imagery of "blockers" or reasons against suicide (e.g., impact on pets/loved ones, impact on self if attempt is non-lethal such as permanent disability).
Imagery depicting suicide as a solution to a problem or goal to be worked towards ('solution imagery') was more evenly distributed across attempts and non-attempts (Table 7).
text.formatted: Imagery depicting suicide as a solution to a problem or goal to be worked towards ('solution imagery') was more evenly distributed across attempts and non-attempts (Table <ref type="table">7</ref>).

text.text: Solution imagery conveyed a sense of action and depicted wanted impacts that suicide was believed to offer as a solution for self or others.

This typically included positive impacts on others, such as imagery of loved ones (spouse, children, parents, friends) being relieved from burden, happier, and financially secure (e.g., buying a house).
For one participant this imagery also included wanted negative impacts on others (suffering and guilt to be experienced by emotionally abusive family).
Solution imagery was appraised as offering freedom, hope, peace, escape from one's own struggles or negative emotions, or as a solution for others (e.g., unburdening others).

Some participants interpreted their suicide imagery as a reflection or realisation of the extent to which they were struggling at that time ("It's my mind, my whole body telling me something is not right."), although this appraisal was typically not associated with an attempt.
The perceived function was often reported as planning or preparation to suicide, although differentially across cases.

Imagery prior to attempt was described as preparing oneself to enact an already-decided plan ("to prepare myself for what I was going to do") or to motivate towards suicide to solve problems (e.g., "to make me do it, in a way.", "for fear" [of consequences if don't attempt]).
Non-attempt imagery was more centred around forming the plan (e.g., "It was about planning.
It was about problem solving.
It was outcome driven.
It was focused on practicalities"; "…I start thinking [about] how would I do this").

Solution imagery prior to attempt was sometimes reported to serve a soothing or relieving function that was centred around anticipation of imminently enacting suicide ("relief to me because I had a way out", "comforting, controlling thought of this will be the outcome").
This contrasts with Mental Exercise Imagery where soothing is derived from the act of imaginal rehearsal, rather than anticipation of imminent behaviour.
Imagery depicting suicide as a mental exercise or fantasy that provides feelings of control or relief ('mental exercise imagery') was almost exclusively reported on non-attempts.

Mental exercise imagery content centred around mentally simulated feelings ("this fantasy of how I would feel") with a focus on the cessation of negative feelings or events for the self, and the term "relief" was used often.
This imagery was perceived to represent control, agency, or choice ("this was my way of gaining control", "the sense of control that this is something I can choose to do or choose not to do").
Mental exercise imagery often described methods that were fantastical, romanticised death, not aligned with real-world details, vague, or less lethal.

Examples included imagined methods ("…this weird contraption thing…"), imagined locations, or locations that no longer exist (e.g. childhood buildings that are now renovated or located internationally).
Romanticised imagery was sometimes described as a "fantasy", daydream, or "imaginary plane".

Participants described the perceived function of this imagery as an emotion regulation or coping strategy wherein the act of mentally simulating suicide provided soothing or relief ("that image did…make me have a better control of the emotions"; "a coping mechanism"; "the function was soothing").
This relief was derived from the act of imagining.
One participant described the coping nature as a form of expression that "allowed me to express my need to die without having to take that out of my mind into the open world for everyone to see".
Imagery discouraging suicide ('discouraging imagery') was primarily associated with nonattempt instances and to a lesser extent aborted attempts.

This imagery commonly depicted the unwanted impact of suicide on other people, with participants conveying that even during their suicidal distress they had the capacity to experience deep care and compassion for others, including both loved ones and strangers (e.g., bystanders).

Content included immediate impacts (e.g. first responders, witnesses, finding the body, loved ones being distressed when informed of the death), medium-term impacts (e.g. mourning and funeral imagery), and long-term impacts such as dependent loved ones (e.g., children, pets) struggling at key milestones or missing the deceased.
Discouraging imagery also depicted unwanted impacts for the self, including injuries and future consequences of non-lethal attempts, or the discomfort of dying.
Some participants reported imagery of their body after lethal suicide behaviour.
Non-attempt instances included distancing references to "the mess" and "the body".

Aborted attempts included detailed and graphic impacts (details omitted due to method dependency), which participants described using more emotive ("carnage"; "confronting"; "pretty f**ked"; "pretty morbid") and less distancing ("what I would look like") language.
Several participants reported that imagery of their body led to imagery about the impact on others who might find their body.

Discouraging imagery included appraisals that suicide would be incongruent with values, traits, reputation, or goals ("I thought that's really inconsistent with …how I see myself"; "It's a really selfish way to go...
I am a very caring person").

For some participants this imagery reflected their decision that suicide is not their chosen option at this time, including imperative language such as "…you need to stay…" and "we're not going through that".
One participant explicitly acknowledged that this imagery "represented ambivalence" and their desire to stay alive at that time.

The perceived function was reported as motivation to not suicide, including references to deciding against suicide ("put some things off the agenda") or finding another path ("me trying to agree with something else").
This included imagery of reasons for living ("my reasons why I definitely wouldn't") that focused on loved ones ("my friend"; "my cats").

A subset of imagery that was only reported on non-attempt instances reflected the experience of considering multiple suicide methods without selecting or committing to enacting a specific suicide action ('consideration imagery').

This involved weighing up options for several suicide methods without choosing one ("weighing up options"; "the various methods") and sometimes included imagined barriers to lethality (e.g., literal barriers or responder intervention).

Some participants appraised the imagery with detached observation ("just a stupid intrusive thought") and perceived the function as an automatic (and potentially conditioned) response to distress, without current functional utility.
One participant reported that their consideration imagery on a non-attempt episode later changed to a single action script prior to attempt.
This study was the first to explore the characteristics of suicide imagery across cases of suicide behaviour.

We extended existing explorations of suicide imagery (De Rozario et al., 2021) by clearly describing five key themes: (a) Determination imagery depicting single method action scripts, (b) Solution imagery highlighting wanted impacts, (c) Mental Exercise or fantasy imagery, (d) Discouraging imagery highlighting unwanted impacts, and (e) Consideration imagery exploring different methods.

text.text: We then systematically explored these themes in relation to the presence or absence of suicide behaviour.

Although others found that suicide imagery may at times be alternately encouraging or discouraging (Hales et al., 2011), we advanced understanding by clearly describing imagery that were most closely associated with attempt behaviour (Determination and Solution Imagery) versus those less associated with attempt behaviour (Mental Exercise, Discouraging, and Consideration Imagery).

text.text: We suggest that future investigations may conceptualise suicide imagery subtypes along two dimensions representing facilitation and deterrence of suicide behaviour, as well as the interaction between these dimensions (Figure 1).
text.formatted: We suggest that future investigations may conceptualise suicide imagery subtypes along two dimensions representing facilitation and deterrence of suicide behaviour, as well as the interaction between these dimensions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This conceptualisation is not intended to present a comprehensive theoretical model of suicide imagery or suicide behaviour risk, but rather a tool to encourage consideration of suicide imagery factors.
The barrier icon acknowledges non-imagery factors (e.g., helper intervention) that may interrupt or prevent attempt behaviour despite strong Facilitating and weak Deterring imagery.
We suggest that Determination and Solution imagery warrant investigation as potential facilitators.
Both subtypes explicitly focused upon working towards suicide as a goal and were associated with suicide behaviour.

Determination imagery aligns well with 'flash-forward' imagery (Holmes et al., 2007), which has been used to refer to suicide imagery more broadly (Hales et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2016; Schultebraucks et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Determination imagery aligns well with 'flash-forward' imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Holmes et al., 2007)</ref>, which has been used to refer to suicide imagery more broadly <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hales et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ng et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Schultebraucks et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In our sample, Determination Imagery was characterised by a detailed single-action method script, a sense of pre-experiencing this method, and resignation or determination to imminently enact it.
These characteristics align with the rich sensory details and perceived "nowness" that prompted Holmes and colleagues to draw parallels between suicide imagery and post-traumatic flashbacks.

This theme is also consistent with the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model's(IMV) account of suicide imagery as a volitional factor that influences suicide behaviour through cognitive rehearsal (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: This theme is also consistent with the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model's(IMV) account of suicide imagery as a volitional factor that influences suicide behaviour through cognitive rehearsal (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).

text.text: The single action scripts are also consistent with the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide's (IPT; Joiner, 2005) suggestion that rehearsal imagery may contribute to acquired capability.
text.formatted: The single action scripts are also consistent with the Interpersonal Theory of <ref type="bibr">Suicide's (IPT;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Joiner, 2005)</ref> suggestion that rehearsal imagery may contribute to acquired capability.

text.text: However, we also identified Solution Imagery as a second facilitator theme precipitating attempt behaviour.
This imagery was perceived as motivating to suicide, assisting method planning, and providing relief in the anticipation that problems would soon be solved via suicide.

Solution Imagery may play a role in enhancing motivation by amplifying perceived desirability of suicide behaviour, consistent with Elaborated Intrusion Theory's (May et al., 2015) assertion that imagery-based elaborations of desired states (in this case relief through suicide) increase motivation for behaviour.
text.formatted: Solution Imagery may play a role in enhancing motivation by amplifying perceived desirability of suicide behaviour, consistent with Elaborated Intrusion Theory's <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(May et al., 2015)</ref> assertion that imagery-based elaborations of desired states (in this case relief through suicide) increase motivation for behaviour.

text.text: Solution imagery included an unexpected instance of wanted negative impacts on others, specifically imagery of estranged family members to experience distress and dishonour in relation to the participant's suicide.
Revenge imagery has been previously documented and associated with increased suicidality (Selby et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Revenge imagery has been previously documented and associated with increased suicidality <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Selby et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: We suggest that Discouraging Imagery and Consideration Imagery warrant investigation as potential deterrents of suicide behaviour.
Both themes explicitly focused on barriers to suicide and were rarely associated with suicide behaviour.
We do not propose Mental Exercise Imagery as a potential deterrent because this imagery portrayed suicide as desirable and did not depict barriers.
The dimension of deterrence from suicide is related to but distinct from the established phenomenon of 'Wish to Live'.
Previous work has highlighted possession of rich reasons to live as a potential protective factor against suicide (for a discussion, see Ernst et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous work has highlighted possession of rich reasons to live as a potential protective factor against suicide (for a discussion, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Ernst et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, some of the Discouraging Imagery described in our sample included depictions of the negative consequences of suicide upon reasons for living (e.g., distress for family, friends, or pets).
However, the focus of deterrence imagery was dissuading away from suicide, rather than engagement towards life.

This delineation between considering the reasons for and against two choices (in this case, suicide versus living) as separate decisions is clinically common, and part of the key DBT skill of 'Pros and Cons' (Linehan, 2015) where the reasons for and against both acting and not acting on crisis urges are charted separately.
text.formatted: This delineation between considering the reasons for and against two choices (in this case, suicide versus living) as separate decisions is clinically common, and part of the key DBT skill of 'Pros and Cons' <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Linehan, 2015)</ref> where the reasons for and against both acting and not acting on crisis urges are charted separately.

text.text: Thus, we suggest that the dimension of deterrence from suicide is distinct from the concept of Wish to Live.
We chose to represent facilitation and deterrence as distinct but interacting dimensions, as variability in one was not entirely dependent on the strength of the other.
Within a single episode, participants could experience a combination of both facilitative and deterring imagery.

We suggest that the interaction between facilitating and deterring imagery warrants investigation as a potential contributor to ambivalence, wherein the co-occurrence of strongly facilitative imagery (e.g., Determination Imagery) alongside strong deterrence imagery (e.g., Discouraging Imagery) might interact to produce high levels of ambivalence, similar to the tensions between Wish to Live and Wish To Die (Ernst et al., 2024).

text.text: Given emerging evidence that ambivalence between co-occurring wish to live and wish to die may present a vulnerability factor for suicide behaviour (Ernst et al., 2024), future research might investigate whether ambivalence between facilitation and deterrence imagery is similarly implicated.

text.text: Imagery prior to attempt was often deliberately constructed, wanted/welcome, and contained content derived from media or personal experience.
Although some participants reported brief imagery flashes of less than a minute, the median imagery duration prior to attempt was 90 minutes.
This suggests that suicide imagery may be acceptable, comforting, or even sought after for some individuals prior to an attempt.
This aligns with findings that prior history of suicidality is associated with greater comfort and less distress during worst-point suicide imagery (Crane et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This aligns with findings that prior history of suicidality is associated with greater comfort and less distress during worst-point suicide imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Crane et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Some suicide imagery may be less closely related to intrusive and distressing trauma imagery than initially posited (Holmes et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Some suicide imagery may be less closely related to intrusive and distressing trauma imagery than initially posited <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Holmes et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, other participants in our sample experienced imagery that was distressing, intrusive, and unwanted prior to attempting suicide, suggesting that clinicians should be cautious not to discount the severity of risk based on individuals' emotional experience of their imagery, because presentations prior to attempt may vary.
Finally, one-quarter of participants in this study had little-to-no verbal ideation.

Although the impact of assessing and modifying suicidal mental imagery on subsequent behaviour is yet to be tested, our findings may hold important implications for supporting people experiencing suicide imagery.

Firstly, it may be valuable for clinicians to assess for suicide imagery to ensure that individuals who do not experience verbal ideation and would not otherwise spontaneously report imagery are detected and supported.
Existing tools for suicide risk assessment such as the C-SSRS (Posner et al., 2011) and SIDAS (van Spijker et al., 2014) assess only verbal ideation.
text.formatted: Existing tools for suicide risk assessment such as the C-SSRS <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Posner et al., 2011) and</ref> <ref type="bibr">SIDAS (van Spijker et al., 2014)</ref> assess only verbal ideation.

text.text: As a result, individuals who experience mental imagery of suicide with minimal verbal ideation may remain undetected.
Secondly, it may be beneficial for clinicians to assess for both facilitating and deterring imagery as distinct dimensions that may separately inform case formulation.
Example questions have been provided in Table 8 to assist clinicians in doing so.

text.text: The impact of such imagery on suicide behaviour is yet to be validated prospectively and these questions do not assess risk of behaviour.
Given calls to develop interventions for suicide imagery (Paulik et al., 2023), these findings demonstrate that suicide imagery is not homogenous.

text.text: There may be variability in the extent to which subtypes are facilitative or deterring of suicide so interventions should be applied cautiously to avoid blanket targeting of suicide imagery as a unitary construct.
Finally, suicide imagery should be re-evaluated regularly as it can change over time.
Although our focus on qualitative interviews allowed for a rich understanding of suicide imagery types and their relationship to suicide behaviour, limitations must be considered.

First, while there was some heterogeneity in this sample in gender, sexuality, and neurotype, the use of online recruitment and participation methods may limit generalizability to groups most susceptible to digital access barriers such as older, lower income, minority, and non-English speaking participants (Alkureishi et al., 2021).

text.text: Second, the findings in this study rely upon retrospective data collected at a single timepoint, which limits causal inference.

Real-time longitudinal research is needed to objectively map the relationships between types of imagery, how they may change over time, and the functional impact of this imagery on suicide behaviour and coping.
Future studies might utilise Ecological Momentary Assessment to reduce reliance on retrospective recall.
It is also important to note limitations with respect to predictive utility.
Although we provide a description of suicide imagery themes that depict potential facilitators and deterrents to suicide, we do not argue that imagery alone is predictive of suicide behaviour.
The prediction of suicide behaviour is inherently complex, impacted by a variety of factors, and notoriously inaccurate (Kessler et al., 2020).

text.text: Instead, we present a preliminary account of suicide imagery themes that warrant further evaluation as potential contributors within the broader context of factors which may influence suicide behaviour.
This study provides a description of varied suicide imagery themes and a framework for conceptualising suicide imagery themes along dimensions of facilitation and deterrence to suicide.
Findings hold important implications for existing theories of suicidality as well as clinical care for people who experience this distressing and risk-increasing symptom.
However, further longitudinal research with larger samples is required to allow for causal inferences to be made regarding the functional impact of imagery types on suicide behaviour.
